children.name: Project title
children.text: Evaluating the Robustness of Classical Machine Learning in Cross-Subject EEG Seizure Detection

children.name: Project description
children.text: A classical ML pipeline trained on 3.5M+ EEG windows to test whether seizure detection still works on patients the model has never seen. Presented at BIOXPLORE 2026 (IEEE & Scopus-indexed).

children.name: Type value
children.text: Research Paper / Machine Learning Study, IEEE Conference

children.name: Result value
children.text: Presented at BIOXPLORE 2026 (IEEE Conference No. 68070X, Bantul, 5 August 2026). Indexed by IEEE & Scopus.

children.name: Overview text
children.text: Epilepsy affects millions of people, and EEG interpretation still depends on specialists reviewing recordings by hand, which is slow and hard to scale. Many published models report near-perfect accuracy, but they are often tested on data from the same patients they trained on.

children.name: Overview text
children.text: This project is our research submission to BIOXPLORE 2026. We ask a harder question: how well do classical machine learning models work on completely unseen patients?

children.name: Problem description
children.text: Seizure windows make up only 0.067% of the data, and every patient's brain signals look different. Under these conditions, accuracy and ROC-AUC can make a useless model look excellent.

children.name: Solution description
children.text: We built a strict, leak-free evaluation pipeline. It combines subject-wise splitting, Leave-One-Subject-Out validation, and AUC-PR as the primary metric. We used it to benchmark four classical models under realistic deployment conditions. We did not propose a new algorithm. Instead, we provide an honest empirical baseline.

children.name: Problem description
children.text: To see why seizure detection breaks in practice, we looked at the CHB-MIT scalp EEG data and measured how hard the task is.

children.text: Three things make this task difficult:

children.name: Metric 1 description
children.text: A model that always predicts "no seizure" is right 99.9% of the time.

children.name: Metric 1 description
children.text: Different patients produce different EEG patterns, so a model that works on one patient often fails on another.

children.name: Metric 1 description
children.text: High accuracy or ROC-AUC does not mean good seizure detection.

children.name: Problem summary
children.text: The problem is not a lack of models or accuracy scores. It is the lack of evaluation that reflects real clinical conditions.

children.name: Goals text
children.text: Reliable seizure detection needs honest evaluation before it needs a bigger model. We set out to test three hypotheses:

children.name: Goals text
children.text:
No significant performance difference exists among classical models for cross-subject detection.
Severe class imbalance degrades detection performance.
Accuracy alone is insufficient for evaluating seizure detection.

children.name: Goals text
children.text:
A reliable baseline for future patient-independent EEG research.
Evidence that clinically meaningful metrics should replace accuracy-only reporting.
Guidance on models that fit initial clinical screening, where missed seizures cost more than false alarms.

children.name: Award Title
children.text: "How well do classical machine learning models generalize to completely unseen patients under extreme class imbalance and inter-subject variability?"

children.name: Goals text
children.text: Instead of building a new detector, we built a realistic test bench in six steps.

children.name: Products description
children.text: Raw EEG was filtered with a zero-phase, 4th-order Butterworth band-pass filter at 0.5–40 Hz. The 0.5 Hz cutoff removes baseline wander and sweat artifacts. The 40 Hz cutoff suppresses muscle noise and interference.

children.name: Products description
children.text: Data is split by patient, never by window. Logistic Regression, SVM (RBF), Random Forest, and XGBoost (GPU, Optuna-tuned) were tested. Class weighting and random under-sampling were applied to training data only, to avoid evaluation bias. LOSO validation was run on Logistic Regression, because simple models keep learned weights interpretable.

children.name: Products description
children.text: ROC curves look strong, but PR curves reveal poor detection of the minority seizure class.

children.name: Goals text
children.text:
Random Forest and XGBoost: Accuracy is above 0.998, but recall is zero. They collapsed into predicting only "non-seizure".
Logistic Regression: It caught about 75% of seizure windows and has the highest AUC-PR. The cost is roughly 80,000 false positives, which could cause alarm fatigue for neurologists.
Under-sampling: Recall rose (Random Forest reached 0.9395), but precision fell to about 0.003. The SVM's AUC-PR could not be computed (NaN).
Class weighting: Results stayed close to baseline. Logistic Regression again led with an AUC-PR of 0.0278.
XGBoost tuning: Optuna tuning reached an objective score of 0.3353, yet recall was still zero. Model complexity did not fix the problem.

children.name: Metric 1 description
children.text: Realistic evaluation protocol: Strict subject-wise split and LOSO validation to prevent leakage.

children.name: Metric 1 description
children.text: Proper metrics: AUC-PR as the primary metric, to avoid misleading performance claims.

children.name: Metric 1 description
children.text: Practical insight: Simpler models can outperform complex ones under extreme imbalance.

children.name: Metric 1 description
children.text: Repeated trials and statistical significance tests were not run because of limited compute.

children.name: Metric 1 description
children.text: LOSO was applied only to Logistic Regression.

children.name: Metric 1 description
children.text: Deep learning was intentionally excluded, to keep the comparison controlled and interpretable.

children.name: Conclusion text
children.text: Classical ML struggles with cross-subject seizure detection. Accuracy is unreliable for imbalanced medical data, so AUC-PR should be used instead. Future work will explore autoencoder-based anomaly detection, contrastive learning (Siamese networks), Focal Loss with hard example mining, and repeated LOSO runs with non-parametric significance tests.

children.name: Icon 1 label
children.text: Honest Evaluation: Patient-independent validation, not inflated scores.

children.name: Icon 1 label
children.text: Right Metrics: AUC-PR over accuracy for clinical relevance.

children.name: Icon 3 label
children.text: Next Step: Representation learning and anomaly detection.

children.name: Conclusion summary
children.text: "High accuracy is not detection. Measuring honestly is the first step to saving lives."
